title: Temporal: The Courtroom for Long-Running AI Workflows
excerpt: Your AI workflow will fail halfway one day. Temporal makes sure it picks up where it stopped, retries the broken step and can even wait hours for a human.

image.alt: Think of Temporal as a court coordinator. It doesn't decide what the AI should do; it coordinates the steps, tracks progress, handles retries and makes sure everything completes. 1, the workflow is the plan; 2, activities do the actual work, like a search API, an LLM call or saving to a database; 3, the worker runs the code; 4, the Temporal server keeps the workflow moving, storing state and history and scheduling tasks. Example: search, ask AI, save the answer, and if the AI call times out, retry automatically.

body.text: Your AI app probably started simple:
Then real life happened:

Now the annoying questions show up. What if the LLM fails? What if a server crashes halfway? What if you have to ==wait three hours for a human==? What if one step failed, and you don't want to start the whole thing again?
That's the problem Temporal is built for.
▶ [Watch my 5-minute Temporal demo](#video-W_vLv9bIgnQ)

body.label: Try it yourself: open the Colab notebook
The one idea to remember
body.text: Temporal is a ==durable execution platform==: it keeps long-running workflows going through crashes, retries and long waits. ==temporalio== is the Python SDK your code uses to talk to it.
Think of Temporal as a courtroom

body.alt: Think of Temporal as a court coordinator. It doesn't decide what the AI should do; it coordinates the steps, tracks progress, handles retries and makes sure everything completes. 1, the workflow is the plan; 2, activities do the actual work, like a search API, an LLM call or saving to a database; 3, the worker runs the code; 4, the Temporal server keeps the workflow moving, storing state and history and scheduling tasks. Example: search, ask AI, save the answer, and if the AI call times out, retry automatically.
body.caption: Workflow, Activity, Worker and Server, as a courtroom.

body.text: Picture a judge. The judge doesn't search documents, call witnesses or do the legwork. The judge ==coordinates==: "First this. Then that. If something goes wrong, follow the rules. If we're waiting for someone, pause here and carry on when they arrive."

Temporal works the same way. One thing to be clear on: ==Temporal doesn't make decisions for you==. You write the rules. Temporal makes sure they run to the end, even when things break. It calls this ==durable execution==: your workflow keeps its progress even if workers, networks or servers fail.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Temporal is the coordinator, not the one doing the work.
Workflow = the plan
A Workflow is the overall process, written as code. For example: search, give the result to the LLM, retry if a step fails, return the answer. Here's a minimal version with the real API:

Two small rules hide in there. Every activity call needs a ==timeout==, so Temporal knows when to give up and retry. And workflow code must be ==deterministic==: no random numbers, no network calls, no reading the clock directly. Anything unpredictable goes in an activity. That's what lets Temporal replay a workflow and land in exactly the same place.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: The Workflow is the plan. Keep it predictable.
Activity = the actual work
An Activity is one piece of real-world work: ==search an API, call an LLM, query a database, send an email, process a payment==.
These are exactly the things that can be slow or fail, which is why they're kept separate from the plan. The workflow says "run search", and the activity actually does it.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: If it talks to the outside world, it's an activity.
Worker = the one doing the work
Here's a surprise: the Temporal server ==doesn't run your Python code==. Your Worker does.
Workers are your own programs. They keep asking a ==task queue== for work, run the workflow and activity code, and report back. You can run several workers on the same queue to share the load.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: The server coordinates. Your workers do the running.
Then what is temporalio?

body.alt: Temporal versus temporalio, same ecosystem, different roles. Temporal is the workflow orchestration platform: it runs your steps, retries on failure, handles long waits and keeps going reliably. temporalio is the Python SDK: your Python code defines workflows and activities, temporalio turns them into requests the platform understands, and Temporal runs and coordinates them. Temporal is the platform; temporalio is how Python talks to it.

body.text: This is where the names get confusing. ==Temporal is the platform==. ==temporalio is the Python SDK==, the official library your Python code uses to work with it:

body.code: pip install temporalio

from temporalio import workflow, activity
from temporalio.client import Client
from temporalio.worker import Worker

body.text: It's MIT licensed, needs Python 3.10 or newer, and the latest version is 1.34.0, from 30 September 2026. To try things on your laptop, the Temporal CLI starts a local dev server with temporal server start-dev. There's also Temporal Cloud, a paid hosted version, if you don't want to run the server yourself.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Temporal is the platform. temporalio is how Python talks to it.
What if something fails?

body.alt: What happens when an AI workflow fails. Without Temporal: the user question, search and AI answer work, then saving the result fails because the server crashed, and nobody knows where to continue, so the whole workflow is lost. With Temporal: it tracks progress at each step, retries the failed save automatically, and continues from where it stopped until the result is saved.
body.caption: An illustration, not a real screenshot.

body.text: Say search and RAG worked, but the LLM call failed. With a ==retry policy==, Temporal retries just that activity:

The clever part isn't the retry itself. Temporal keeps an ==event history== of everything that already happened, so it continues from where it stopped instead of starting over. Search doesn't run twice just because the LLM had a bad moment.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Only the failed step runs again. Everything else is remembered.
It can also wait
Say your AI writes a report and a human has to approve it. The workflow can simply ==wait==, for minutes, hours or days, without holding up a server. When the approval arrives, it carries on.
Temporal's [AI cookbook](https://docs.temporal.io/ai-cookbook) has examples of exactly this kind of thing: long-running agents, human-in-the-loop steps and multi-step AI pipelines.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Waiting for a human is just another step.
Where AI fits
Temporal ==isn't the LLM==. It isn't RAG. It isn't an agent framework. It sits around the workflow and keeps it running.

That's why it can be used alongside agent frameworks like [LangGraph](/blog/langgraph-ai-agents-workflow): LangGraph shapes the agent's reasoning and tool steps, and Temporal keeps the bigger process durable. Temporal's docs also show an official integration with the OpenAI Agents SDK.

One honest note: Temporal isn't the only way to do this, and it has a ==learning curve==. For a small script, it's overkill. It earns its place when workflows are long, expensive or can't afford to lose progress.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Agent frameworks shape the thinking. Temporal makes the process survive.

title: CrewAI vs n8n: Stop Comparing Tools. Understand the Difference.
excerpt: CrewAI makes AI agents work together. n8n connects AI to the rest of the world. Here's the difference in 5 minutes, with one real example and when to pick which.

image.alt: CrewAI versus n8n. Left, CrewAI: agents, roles and collaboration in Python code, with a crew.py file defining a researcher, a writer and a reviewer, and an agent flow where they share context. Right, n8n: a visual workflow builder connecting an email trigger, an AI agent, a vector store, an HTTP request and Slack, with node settings and an execution preview. Different starting points, some overlap.

body.text: You've seen it: =="CrewAI vs n8n"==, followed by 20 minutes of feature lists.
Let's make it simpler. Say you want to build this:
There are lots of ways to build it. Two interesting ones are CrewAI and n8n.

body.label: The one idea to remember
body.text: CrewAI asks: =="How do my AI agents collaborate?"== n8n asks: =="How does my AI system connect to the real world?"==
The 10-second difference

body.alt: CrewAI versus n8n, two ways to build AI systems with the same goal. CrewAI, for agent collaboration: a research crew of researcher, writer and reviewer agents with roles, tools and a final output. n8n, for workflows and integrations: a canvas where a form submission flows through an AI agent with a chat model, memory and a search tool, then an HTTP request, Airtable and Gmail.
body.caption: An illustration, not a real screenshot. n8n lists 1500+ integrations today, more than the picture says.

body.text: Think about a team.

**CrewAI** asks: "How can I make ==AI agents work together==?" You write Python and describe agents, their tasks and their tools, then group them into a crew, like a researcher, a writer and a reviewer passing work along. For more control over the order of steps, it also has ==Flows==.
**n8n** asks: "How can I ==connect AI to the rest of the world==?" You build a workflow on a visual canvas, and AI is one step among many.

items.label: CrewAI
items.text: Agent collaboration

items.label: n8n
items.text: Workflows and integrations

body.text: There's overlap. But this mental model gets you ==80% of the way there==.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: CrewAI starts from the agents. n8n starts from the workflow.
One real example: support emails
Imagine you're building ==an AI that reads customer emails and handles support tickets==.
**With CrewAI**, you'd design a team:
The interesting question becomes: ==which agent should do what?==
**With n8n**, you'd design the path the data takes:
Now the interesting question becomes: ==what should happen to the data?==
Same job. Different first question. That's why the tools feel so different.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Agents vs data flow: that's the real difference in practice.
Where n8n gets really nice
Say your workflow breaks somewhere in the middle:

In n8n you can open the ==execution== and see exactly what went into and came out of each node. For someone learning AI engineering, that's huge. You're not staring at "ERROR ERROR ERROR, why". You can ==follow the data==.
This is one reason I personally enjoyed working with n8n, especially for larger workflows and multi-RAG experiments.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Seeing the data move is the fastest way to find a bug.
The catch: visual spaghetti
n8n's canvas is fantastic... until your workflow looks like this:

body.code:
┌── IF
        │    ↓
A → B → C → LOOP → D
        │       ↘
        └→ ERROR → RETRY
                    ↓
                 SUBFLOW

body.text: Then you add 30 more nodes. At some point, ==visual becomes spaghetti==.
That's where code can be easier to maintain. With CrewAI, your logic lives in Python files, so it fits naturally with tests, Git and CI/CD.

items.label: Visual
items.text: Doesn't automatically mean easier.

items.label: Code
items.text: Doesn't automatically mean harder.

body.text: It depends on the ==size and shape== of what you're building.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Small and connected: visual shines. Big and complex: code often wins.
The actual trade-off

body.alt: CrewAI's code editor next to n8n's canvas: Python files define agents with roles, goals and tools on one side; on the other, a visual workflow connects Gmail, an AI agent, a Postgres vector store, an HTTP request and Slack, with an execution preview.
body.caption: An illustration, not a real screenshot.

items.title: Look at CrewAI for
items.text: Agent collaboration, Python development, and large codebases with tests and CI/CD.

items.title: Look at n8n for
items.text: Visual workflows, connecting APIs and apps, webhooks and triggers, visual debugging, and learning by watching data move.

items.title: Both handle
items.text: Structured workflows. CrewAI has Flows; n8n is built around workflows.

body.text: It's ==not a leaderboard==. Just different strengths.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Pick by the shape of your problem, not by the hype.
Don't become "an n8n guy"

body.alt: Different frameworks, same building blocks. An AI system is made of an LLM for reasoning, tools, RAG for your data, memory, routing, loops, agents and observability. CrewAI assembles them with agent collaboration and roles, n8n assembles them graphically with workflows and integrations, and LangGraph assembles them as a stateful graph with custom logic. Tools change, concepts stay.
body.caption: The LangGraph code here is simplified. The full version is in our LangGraph post.

body.text: Don't be the person who says "I'm an n8n guy" or "CrewAI is the only way". Frameworks change ==fast==. What's underneath them doesn't:
Once you understand those, picking up a new framework is ==way easier==.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Tools change. Concepts stay.
The best way to learn

body.alt: Build an AI research assistant two ways. In CrewAI, agents work together: a researcher searches for papers, an analyst extracts insights, a writer writes the report and a reviewer checks it. In n8n, a workflow runs daily: get papers over HTTP from arXiv, create embeddings and search, an AI agent analyses and writes, the report is formatted and emailed. Same goal, two approaches.
body.caption: An illustration, not a real screenshot.

body.text: Don't watch "CrewAI vs n8n vs LangGraph vs Framework X" for three hours. ==Build something.==
Take one tiny project, like an AI research assistant, and build it three times:
You'll quickly notice:

items: how each one represents the workflow
where each approach starts to feel uncomfortable

body.text: And suddenly you're not learning frameworks. You're learning ==AI engineering==.

body.label: New to LangGraph? Read the LangGraph post
Takeaway
body.text: One small project, three frameworks. You'll learn more than any comparison video.
Remember this

body.label: Remember

title: LangGraph: How AI Agents Actually Follow a Workflow
excerpt: An LLM gives an answer. An agent gets a job done. Here's how LangGraph turns steps, decisions, state and loops into an agent, with a tiny AI debugger you can run in Colab.

image.alt: How AI agents actually follow a workflow: LangGraph lets you build an agent as a graph of connected steps. 1, user input "Find the bug in this code"; 2, think; 3, use a tool; 4, check the result; 5, decide if the task is complete; if no, 7, retry and loop back; if yes, 6, done. A simplified code panel shows StateGraph with add_node calls. Key idea: node is a step, edge is a path, loop is try again.

body.text: You've heard it everywhere: "We can build AI agents using LangGraph."
Sounds fancy. But what is LangGraph actually doing? Do we really need another framework just to call an LLM?
Let's skip the scary diagrams and build the idea from one tiny problem.
▶ [Watch my 4-minute LangGraph demo](#video-SiZb22_2pe0)

body.label: Try it yourself: open the Colab notebook
The one idea to remember
body.text: The ==LLM is the brain==. ==LangGraph is the workflow==: it decides which step runs next, carries the state between steps, and loops back when something fails.
Imagine your AI has a job
You tell an AI coding assistant: =="My code is broken. Find the bug and fix it."==
A normal LLM looks at the code and says, "Found it. You used - instead of +." Cool. But an actual coding agent has to do more than point:

body.repeat: If not, fix and test again

body.text: That's not one answer anymore. That's a ==workflow==. And this is where LangGraph comes in.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Doing a job takes steps, checks and retries, not one reply.
So what is LangGraph?
LangGraph is a framework for building AI agents as ==workflows made of steps, decisions, state and loops==. That's it.

Don't let "framework" scare you. It just means a structure that saves you from building every piece from zero. LangGraph's own [description](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) is a "low-level orchestration framework for building stateful agents". In plain words: ==the LLM provides the intelligence, LangGraph organises what happens next==.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: LangGraph is the workflow manager for your AI agent.
LLM vs AI agent

body.alt: Normal LLM versus AI agent. A normal LLM takes a question, "How do I cancel my subscription?", and gives a direct answer. An AI agent takes a goal, "Cancel my subscription and confirm it for me", then thinks, uses tools such as a browser or APIs, checks the result, decides whether the goal is done, tries again if not, and finishes. An LLM gives an answer; an AI agent gets things done.

body.text: A normal LLM is simple: you ask, it answers, done.
An agent works towards a goal:
An agent isn't "ask AI, get answer". It's a ==process==, and LangGraph helps you build that process.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: An LLM gives an answer. An agent gets the job done.
Why is it called a graph?

body.alt: A graph is a workflow. A coding example: diagnose the code (def add returns a minus b, a bug), run the test (expected 5, got -1), check whether it passed; if no, fix the code (return a plus b) and run the tests again; if yes, done. Key concepts: a node is a step, an edge is a path, a decision chooses the next path, a loop means try again.

body.text: Forget the maths-class meaning. Here a graph is just ==connected steps==, like A → B → C.
Our debugger as a graph: diagnose, test, then a decision. Passed? Done. Failed? Fix, and test again.
Different steps, different paths. Sometimes the workflow moves forward, sometimes it ==goes back==, and sometimes it decides.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: A graph is a flowchart your agent actually follows.
The 4 things you need to understand
Forget the 50-page docs for now. Start with these four:

items.title: Node = a step
items.text: One thing your agent does: diagnose, test or fix. Think "do this job".

items.title: Edge = the path
items.text: The arrow from one node to the next. Think "go here next".

items.title: State = what it carries
items.text: The info passed along: the buggy code, the diagnosis, the test result, how many attempts, the fixed code.

items.title: Conditional edge = a decision
items.text: Where to go based on what happened. Test passed? Done. Failed? Back to fix.

body.text: Put a conditional edge after a test and you get the best part: a ==loop==. Instead of Step 1 → 2 → 3 → finish, you can say "if it isn't good enough, go back and try again". That's much closer to how useful agents actually work.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Nodes, edges, state, decisions. Add a loop and you have an agent.
Our tiny AI debugger

body.alt: A tiny AI coding debugger built with LangGraph and Sarvam. LangGraph controls the workflow; Sarvam is the reasoning model. The developer says "My code is broken. Find the bug and fix it"; LangGraph runs the steps; Sarvam finds the bug; state stores the code, diagnosis, test result and fix attempts; the test checks add(2, 3) equals 5; if it fails, Sarvam suggests changing return a - b to return a + b and the test runs again; when it passes, the agent returns the fixed code.

body.text: Our broken code is ridiculously simple:

body.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a - b

body.text: We expect add(2, 3) to give 5. It gives ==-1==. Test failed, bug found. Now let's see who does what.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: A tiny bug is perfect for watching the whole workflow run.
Where Sarvam fits

Important: ==LangGraph is not the LLM==. In our experiment the thinking is done by [Sarvam](https://docs.sarvam.ai/)'s sarvam-105b, a model from an Indian AI company. LangGraph runs the workflow around it. Here's the conversation, roughly:

items.label: Sarvam
items.text: "I think the problem is a - b."

items.label: LangGraph
items.text: "Okay. Now let's test it."

items.label: Test
items.text: "Still broken."

items.label: LangGraph
items.text: "Then go back and fix it."

items.label: LangGraph
items.text: "We're done."

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Sarvam thinks. LangGraph decides what happens next.
What LangGraph actually gives you

Without a workflow framework, you write a growing pile of logic by hand: call the model, check the response, run a tool, check again, call the model again, maybe retry, maybe run another tool... As the agent grows, that pile gets ==hard to manage==.
LangGraph makes the workflow explicit instead. Here's our debugger wired up with the real API. The three step functions are left short; the full version is in the Colab.

body.code:
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END

class State(TypedDict):
    code: str
    diagnosis: str
    passed: bool
    attempts: int

def diagnose(state): ...  # Sarvam reads the code and explains the bug
def test(state): ...      # runs add(2, 3) and checks it equals 5
def fix(state): ...       # Sarvam rewrites the code

def route(state):
    # Stop when the test passes, or after 3 tries so it can't loop forever
    return "done" if state["passed"] or state["attempts"] >= 3 else "fix"

graph = StateGraph(State)
graph.add_node("diagnose", diagnose)
graph.add_node("test", test)
graph.add_node("fix", fix)
graph.add_edge(START, "diagnose")
graph.add_edge("diagnose", "test")
graph.add_conditional_edges("test", route, {"fix": "fix", "done": END})
graph.add_edge("fix", "test")

app = graph.compile()
result = app.invoke({"code": "def add(a, b):\n    return a - b", "attempts": 0})

body.text: Read it top to bottom and you can see the whole agent: the state, three nodes, the edges, one decision, and a loop from fix back to test.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Nodes + edges + state + decisions + loops, instead of a pile of if-statements.
The mental model

body.alt: LangGraph as the AI agent workflow at the centre: the LLM is the brain that reasons; tools are things it can use, like web search, code execution, databases and APIs; state is the information it carries, like user input, previous steps and tool results; decisions choose what happens next; loops try again until the result is right; together they complete the task.

body.label: Remember
body.text: The ==LLM is the brain==. ==LangGraph is the workflow==: it decides which step runs next, carries the state between steps, and loops back when something fails.

body.text: Brain + tools + state + decisions + loops = an AI agent.

Theory is nice, but you'll get LangGraph much faster by watching it run. We built this little LangGraph and Sarvam debugger in Colab. In it, you'll:

Final thought
Don't think of LangGraph as ==another AI framework to memorise==. Think: "I have an AI that needs to finish a task. LangGraph helps me design the path it follows."

items.label: A workflow

title: RAG-Anything: RAG That Can Understand More Than Text
excerpt: Basic RAG reads text. Real knowledge also lives in images, tables and videos. Here's how RAG-Anything connects them, and a small PDF-plus-video experiment you can try.

image.alt: Text-only RAG versus multimodal documents. Left, the traditional way: PDF, text extraction, embeddings, search, LLM, and what gets lost: details in images, table structure, diagrams and video content, so answers are based only on text. Right, the real world: documents mix text, images, tables, diagrams and video, so a multimodal pipeline processes each type (for example with Docling or MinerU), retrieves across all of them and lets an LLM answer using everything, not just text.

body.text: You probably know the basic RAG flow by now:
Pretty simple. But what if your information ==isn't just text==? What if it's a PDF with charts, a screenshot, a table, a lecture video or a voice note?
That's where things get messy, and where RAG-Anything gets interesting.
▶ [Watch my 6-minute RAG-Anything demo](#video-7KQZ4VNqlS4)

body.label: Try it yourself: open the Colab notebook
The one idea to remember
body.text: RAG-Anything doesn't cram everything into ==one giant embedding==. Each type of content is ==understood its own way==, then connected into ==one searchable knowledge base==.
A PDF and a video walk into a RAG app
Imagine you upload two files:

body.code:
RAG.pdf                 the PDF explains RAG
RAG-explanation.mp4     the video demonstrates it

body.text: Then you ask: =="Does the video actually demonstrate what the PDF explains?"==
A text-only RAG app is stuck. It can read the PDF, but the video is invisible to it. To answer, your app has to understand ==two different kinds of content== and connect them.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Real questions often span more than one kind of content.
The old way: a lot of wires
Without a framework, you build a separate path for every type of content:

items: **PDF:** a parser like Docling or MinerU
**Everything:** embeddings, a vector database, a retriever and an LLM

body.text: That's ==a lot of wires==. You become the person connecting every tool to every other tool, and fixing it every time one of them changes.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Multimodal RAG by hand works, but the plumbing is the hard part.
RAG-Anything's idea

body.alt: RAG-Anything as an orchestration layer that connects different tools and data types for multimodal RAG. Inputs: PDFs and documents, images, tables, video, audio and other formats. It uses tools for document extraction (Docling, MinerU), image understanding, table parsing, audio processing and chunking, and runs three steps: understand each type, retrieve across all of them, and answer.
body.caption: In the real library, the inputs are documents, images, tables and equations. We handle video ourselves, in Part 4.

body.text: [RAG-Anything](https://github.com/HKUDS/RAG-Anything) is an open-source framework from the HKUDS lab at the University of Hong Kong. Instead of you wiring every tool together, it runs the whole multimodal pipeline: it ==parses the document==, ==understands each part== (text, images, tables, equations) and ==connects them== into one knowledge base you can ask questions about.

It's built on [LightRAG](https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG), which stores knowledge as a graph: things and how they relate. For parsing it plugs in tools you may already know, [MinerU](/blog/mineru-document-parsing-for-beginners) or [Docling](/blog/docling-pdf-is-not-just-text). It reads PDFs, Office files and images.

body.label: Not an "OpenAI wrapper"
body.text: RAG-Anything isn't just a thin layer over one AI model. It's the ==glue== that coordinates the parser, the vision model, the text model and the knowledge base, and you choose which models to plug in.
Status, checked on 1 Oct 2026: it's MIT licensed and actively updated. The latest release on [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/raganything/) is 1.4.1, from 2 September 2026.

body.code: pip install 'raganything[all]'

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: RAG-Anything is the glue between the tools, so you don't have to be.
What about video?

body.alt: From video to searchable knowledge in five steps: 1, a 10-minute video; 2, find important moments from scene changes or slides; 3, pick three frames, at 2:15 (what RAG is), 5:40 (chunking) and 8:30 (retrieval); 4, a vision-language model looks at each frame, reads any text and understands what's happening; 5, each frame becomes a text description stored for RAG. Don't send thousands of frames: a 10-minute video can have 18,000 or more.
body.caption: Three frames, three descriptions. That's the whole trick.

body.text: One honest note first: RAG-Anything ==doesn't take video files directly==. So we do the video part ourselves, and it's simpler than it sounds.

Do we send the whole video to an expensive video AI? No. We ==pick a few important moments==, grab one frame from each, and ask a vision model: "What is happening here?" Each answer becomes a short description, and those descriptions are what we search.

body.label: Why only 3 frames?
body.text: A 10-minute video has thousands of frames. At 30 frames a second, that's 18,000. We're learning, not ==burning money==, so 3 useful frames are plenty. Smarter frame picking can come later.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Turn a video into a few pictures, and the pictures into words.
Our experiment

body.alt: PDF plus video into connected knowledge. A Machine Learning Basics PDF is processed into text chunks; a Gradient Descent video gives a few important frames that a vision model turns into visual chunks with captions. Both go into one connected knowledge base. The question "What does the PDF explain, and does the video demonstrate it?" retrieves text and visual chunks, and the answer says the PDF explains gradient descent and the video demonstrates it step by step.

body.text: Here's the plan:

items: **The PDF** goes through RAG-Anything's normal document pipeline.
**The video** becomes 3 frames. Each one goes in as an image with a caption saying which moment it is.
Then we ask one question across both: =="What does the PDF explain, and does the video demonstrate it?"==

Grabbing a frame is one command per moment with ffmpeg:

body.text: And this is the RAG-Anything part. It assumes you've already set up RAG-Anything with your chosen models, as in the project's README:

    {"type": "image", "img_path": "/abs/path/frame_0215.jpg",
     "image_caption": ["Video at 2:15: what RAG is"], "page_idx": 0},
    {"type": "image", "img_path": "/abs/path/frame_0540.jpg",

Why this is powerful
The PDF might say: "RAG retrieves relevant documents before generating an answer."
The video might show it happening on screen:
On their own, each one tells half the story. Connected, your system can say =="yes, the video demonstrates exactly what the PDF explains"==, and point to both.

The one thing to remember

title: ColBERT: When Normal Semantic Search Isn't Enough
excerpt: A 10-minute beginner journey from embeddings to ColBERT to RAG: why matching word by word can find the passage that normal semantic search misses.

image.alt: Semantic search versus ColBERT. Left, semantic search works at chunk level: the whole query "How many days can I cancel my annual subscription?" becomes one vector and is compared with one vector per chunk, so it asks "Is this whole chunk about my question?". Right, ColBERT works at token level with late interaction: every word of the query gets its own representation and is matched with words in the passage, such as cancel, annual, subscription and days, giving a relevance score; it asks "Which parts of this passage match my question?".

body.text: You have 1,000 pages of documents. Someone asks one very specific question. Somewhere in there is the one paragraph that answers it. How does a RAG app find it?
Most apps start with semantic search, and it works well most of the time. This post is about the times it doesn't, and about ColBERT, a way of searching that looks closer.

body.label: The one idea to remember
body.text: Semantic search looks at the ==whole chunk==. ColBERT looks at the ==important words== in your question and matches them with words in the document.
The problem: finding the right piece
In a RAG app, the AI doesn't read all 1,000 pages every time. First, a ==retriever== picks a handful of pieces that look relevant. Then the AI answers using only those pieces.
So the answer can only be as good as the pieces the retriever picked. If it misses the paragraph with the answer, the AI never sees it.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Good answers start with finding the right pieces.
How normal semantic search works

body.alt: Dense semantic search in five steps: 1, the user asks "How many days can I cancel my annual subscription?"; 2, an embedding model turns it into a dense vector; 3, one query vector represents the whole question; 4, similarity search compares it with each chunk's vector (scores 0.92, 0.78, 0.31, 0.18); 5, the top chunks, about subscription policy and billing, are returned and passed to the LLM.

body.text: Semantic search turns your question into ==one vector==, a list of numbers that captures its overall meaning. Every chunk of your documents gets one vector too. The search returns the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question's.

That's great for ==broad meaning==. But take the question "How many days can I cancel my annual subscription?" Lots of chunks are about subscriptions: billing, renewals, monthly plans, cancelling. Semantic search can tell they're all on topic. It's less good at noticing which one mentions the 30 days you actually asked about.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Semantic search finds chunks about the same topic, not always the one with the detail.
Enter ColBERT: matching word by word

body.alt: ColBERT finds relevant passages by comparing tokens, in six steps: 1, the question is split into tokens (how, many, days, can, I, cancel, my, annual, subscription); 2, each query token gets its own context-aware vector; 3, the document passage is split into tokens with vectors too; 4, late interaction: each query token is matched with its most similar document token (days with 30, cancel with cancel, annual with annual, subscription with subscription); 5, the best matches combine into one relevance score, 0.92; 6, passages are ranked by score.

body.text: ColBERT keeps a vector for ==every word== (strictly, every token), and each one is shaped by the words around it. When you search, it takes each word in your question, finds the best-matching word in a passage, and adds those matches up into a score. This is called ==late interaction==, because the question and the passage are only compared at search time, word by word.

So for our question, "cancel", "annual", "subscription" and "days" each look for their own match. A passage that says "cancel your annual subscription within 30 days" scores high because every important word finds a partner.

body.label: Remember
body.text: ColBERT doesn't just ask "are these two texts generally similar?" It asks ==which parts of this passage match which parts of my question==.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: ColBERT compares words, not whole chunks.
ColBERT vs normal embeddings

items.title: What gets stored
items.text: Semantic search: one vector per chunk. ColBERT: a vector for every token, each shaped by its context.

items.title: How it matches
items.text: Semantic search: overall meaning. ColBERT: word-by-word matches, added up into a score.

items.title: Complexity
items.text: Semantic search: simpler to set up. ColBERT: more moving parts.

items.title: Storage
items.text: Semantic search: generally smaller. ColBERT: generally larger, since it keeps many vectors per passage.

items.title: Good for
items.text: Semantic search: general retrieval. ColBERT: when fine details in the wording matter.

body.text: One thing to be clear about: ColBERT is ==not automatically better==. It's another way to retrieve, and it earns its extra cost when fine-grained matching matters.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Different tool, different trade-off. Not a straight upgrade.
What is RAGatouille?

body.alt: ColBERT and RAGatouille. ColBERT is a token-level retrieval model; RAGatouille is a Python library that makes ColBERT easier to use, handling indexing and searching. A search for "How many days can I cancel my annual subscription?" returns the subscription policy passage first.
body.caption: The code in this picture is simplified. Use the code in Part 6.

body.text: ==ColBERT is the retrieval model==. ==RAGatouille is a Python library== that makes ColBERT easy to use: you give it documents, it builds the index, and you search it in a few lines.

A quick honest note on its status, checked on 30 Sept 2026. RAGatouille isn't new. Its latest release on [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/ragatouille/) is 0.0.9.post2, from May 2025, and the last change to its [GitHub project](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/RAGatouille) was in the same month. The project isn't archived, but it hasn't been updated since.

body.label: So how should you use it?
body.text: Treat RAGatouille as an easy way to ==learn and try ColBERT==. Before you build something serious on it, check what the current ColBERT tools are.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: ColBERT is the idea. RAGatouille is a handy way to try it.
Try it yourself
Here's a tiny experiment you can run in a notebook. Four short documents:

body.code:
Annual subscription plans are billed every twelve months.
Customers may cancel their annual subscription within 30 days of purchase.
Monthly subscriptions can be cancelled at any time.
Annual plans may renew automatically unless cancellation is requested.

body.text: And one question: "How many days can I cancel my annual subscription?" This is the code, following RAGatouille's own README:

body.code: pip install ragatouille

from ragatouille import RAGPretrainedModel

docs = [
    "Annual subscription plans are billed every twelve months.",
    "Customers may cancel their annual subscription within 30 days of purchase.",
    "Monthly subscriptions can be cancelled at any time.",
    "Annual plans may renew automatically unless cancellation is requested.",
]

RAG = RAGPretrainedModel.from_pretrained("colbert-ir/colbertv2.0")
RAG.index(index_name="subscriptions", collection=docs)

for r in RAG.search("How many days can I cancel my annual subscription?", k=3):
    print(r["rank"], round(r["score"], 2), r["content"])

body.text: You should see the =="within 30 days" sentence ranked first==: it's the one where "cancel", "annual", "subscription" and "days" all find a match. The other sentences are about subscriptions too, so they still show up, just lower.
Your exact scores will vary. What matters is the ranking.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Four sentences are enough to see word-by-word matching at work.
ColBERT doesn't answer the question

body.alt: From many documents to an answer: 1, many documents (research paper, user guide, report, web page) are the knowledge source; 2, ColBERT finds the relevant parts with token-level search for the query "How does photosynthesis work in plants?"; 3, the top matching passages come from different documents; 4, an LLM uses those passages to write a grounded answer and lists its sources.

body.text: This trips up a lot of beginners. ColBERT is a ==retriever==. It finds useful passages. It doesn't write anything.
Writing the answer is the ==LLM's job==. It reads the passages ColBERT found and turns them into a reply.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: ColBERT finds. The LLM answers.
Where Docling and MinerU fit

body.alt: RAG pipeline from documents to answers in seven steps: 1, a real-world PDF; 2, document extraction with Docling or MinerU into structured Markdown; 3, chunking; 4, retrieval with embeddings or ColBERT; 5, the most relevant passages; 6, an LLM that uses the question and passages; 7, a grounded final answer with sources.
body.caption: The whole pipeline. Click to enlarge for the details.

body.text: If you've read our posts on [Docling](/blog/docling-pdf-is-not-just-text) and [Docling and MinerU](/blog/mineru-document-parsing-for-beginners), this is where they connect. Each tool has one job:

items: **Docling or MinerU** turn messy documents into clean, structured text.
**ColBERT** finds the passages that matter for a question.
**The LLM** writes the final answer from those passages.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Better documents in, better passages out, better answers at the end.
The 10-second mental model

body.alt: RAG in three simple steps: 1, prepare: Docling or MinerU turn messy documents into clean, structured text; 2, retrieve: ColBERT finds the most relevant passages for "How many days can I cancel my annual subscription?"; 3, generate: an LLM writes the final answer from those passages.

body.text: If you remember one thing from this series, make it this:
==Docling or MinerU prepare the document. ColBERT finds the useful parts. The LLM explains them.==
When should you care about ColBERT?
ColBERT is worth a look when:

items: your documents are full of detail, like policies, manuals or legal text
questions are specific, and ==small wording differences matter==
normal semantic search keeps returning passages that are on topic but miss the detail
you want to learn how more advanced retrieval works

body.text: But ==don't use it just because it sounds advanced==. For many apps, normal embeddings plus a reranker (a second model that re-sorts the top results) is simpler and good enough.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Start simple. Reach for ColBERT when the details keep getting missed.
The final takeaway
Embeddings give you the ==big picture==. ColBERT gives retrieval a ==finer lens==. And in RAG, better retrieval means the LLM gets better context to work with.

**Also read:** [Your PDF Isn't Just Text](/blog/docling-pdf-is-not-just-text) and [Docling and MinerU: A Simple Guide to Document Parsing](/blog/mineru-document-parsing-for-beginners), the first two parts of this series. Next: [RAG-Anything: RAG That Can Understand More Than Text](/blog/rag-anything-multimodal-rag).

title: Docling and MinerU: A Simple Guide to Document Parsing
excerpt: How does an AI app actually read your PDF? A simple guide to document parsing and two tools that do it, Docling and MinerU, with a free Colab command to try it yourself.

image.alt: MinerU and Docling: two document parsing tools that help AI understand your files. 1, a real-world PDF (the Bitcoin paper) holds headings, paragraphs, images, tables, equations and multiple columns. 2, MinerU and Docling side by side: MinerU has a model-based pipeline with Flash, Basic, Standard and Advanced tiers and a document library for agent-style reading; Docling is a document parsing and conversion tool for PDF, DOCX, PPTX and XLSX that focuses on structured output for RAG. 3, structured output: Markdown, tables, images, equations and clean text. Below, how it fits in an AI pipeline (PDF, MinerU or Docling, structured content, chunking, embeddings, vector database, RAG and LLM) and quick takeaways: both are document parsing tools, use either or both, and see the Docling blog for more.

body.text: You upload a PDF to an AI app and ask, "Summarise this chapter." A few seconds later, you have a summary.
It feels like magic. But how did the AI actually read that PDF? There's an ==important step== that happens before the AI sees a single word, and that's what this post is about.
We'll keep it simple and meet two tools that do this job, **Docling** and **MinerU**.

body.label: New to Docling? Read our Docling post first

body.text: A PDF isn't a clean page of text
A PDF can hold a heading, then a paragraph, then a picture, a table, an equation and another section, all arranged on the page in ==columns and boxes==.
If you simply pull out all the text, that neat page can turn into a blob like this:

body.code:
Electric field...
12.5
Figure 4
E = F/q
current...

body.text: The words are there. ==What they belong to is gone.== Which number goes with which row? Is "Figure 4" a heading? Nobody knows any more, including the AI.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: A PDF is a layout, not a list of words.
What document parsing means
In simple words, ==document parsing== means taking a document and working out ==what's inside it==. Instead of one big pile of text, you get the pieces, each with a label:

items: Heading, paragraph, table, image, section, equation

body.text: The important part isn't just getting the words. It's knowing ==where each word belongs==: this is a title, this is a table cell, this caption goes with that figure.
Our [Docling post](/blog/docling-pdf-is-not-just-text#part-3) shows this step by step, with a real page and every part labelled.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Parsing keeps the shape of the document, not just its words.
Why AI needs this

Say you're building a study app, and a student uploads Physics Chapter 5. Later, the app has to find the right part of that chapter to answer a question. That's ==RAG==: the AI looks things up in your documents before it answers.

If the chapter went in as a blob, the app searches through the blob. If it was parsed first, the app knows the chapter, the section, the equation and the figure, and every piece it finds comes ==with that context==.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Good answers start with a well-parsed document.
Docling and MinerU: same goal, different tools

You may already know **Docling** from [our Docling post](/blog/docling-pdf-is-not-just-text). **MinerU** is in the same category: an open-source document parser, from the OpenDataLab team. You give either one a document, and you get back structured content your app can use.

body.label: Tell the neighbours
body.text: Your neighbour's kid just built a RAG app with Docling, and now the whole colony is talking about it. Relax. You're about to learn MinerU, which does the same job its own way. Next family function, you get to say, "Oh, I tried both."
So which one is right? ==Both.== They solve ==the same problem with different engines==. The simplest way to remember the difference:

items.label: Docling
items.text: "Give me a document and I'll turn it into a structured document object."

items.label: MinerU
items.text: "Give me documents and I'll parse them so an app or an AI agent can read, search and point to exact pages."

body.text: A few basics about MinerU:

items: It reads PDFs and images, and also Word, PowerPoint, Excel, EPUB and HTML files, among others.
It can give you the result as Markdown, HTML, LaTeX and a few other formats.
It runs on your own computer by default. Your documents aren't uploaded anywhere unless you set that up.

body.label: More on Docling
body.text: How it reads layout, handles scanned pages and exports Markdown is all in [our Docling post](/blog/docling-pdf-is-not-just-text).

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Docling and MinerU are neighbours, not rivals. Same job, different engines.
MinerU's four speed settings
MinerU lets you choose how hard it works on a document. It calls these ==tiers==:

items: Basic: adds OCR and small models
Advanced: most effort, for the hardest documents

body.text: Think of it like choosing between ==a quick glance== and ==a careful read==. A simple, clean PDF is fine with Flash. A scanned textbook full of tables and equations is where Standard and Advanced earn their time.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Pick the tier that matches how messy your document is.
Try it yourself

body.alt: How to install, parse and compare with MinerU and Docling in three steps: 1, install the MinerU command line tool with pip install -U mineru; 2, parse bitcoin.pdf with mineru-kit parse --tier standard into bitcoin_standard.md, Markdown with content, tables and structure; 3, compare the MinerU and Docling outputs side by side and choose what works best for your documents. Note: the first run downloads models, that is normal, do not stop it. Python 3.10 to 3.14. The best parser is the one that works on your documents. Test it.

body.text: You can try MinerU for free in Google Colab. Install it, upload a PDF (the classic Bitcoin paper works well), and run one command:

body.code: !pip install -U "mineru>=4.0,<5"
!mineru-kit parse "/content/bitcoin.pdf" -o "/content/bitcoin_standard.md" --tier standard

body.text: The first run downloads some model files, so it can look busy for a while. That's normal. ==Don't stop it== and ==don't run it twice==. When it finishes, open the Markdown file and look for headings, paragraphs, lists and tables.

Then do the fun part: run the same PDF through Docling ([the commands are here](/blog/docling-pdf-is-not-just-text#part-5)) and put the two results side by side. Don't ask "Which tool is better?" Ask =="Which one keeps what I need from my documents?"==

body.label: Good to know
body.text: MinerU needs Python 3.10 to 3.14. Colab's Python works.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: The best parser is the one that works on your documents. Test it.
The one thing to remember
Think of a messy school bag. Books, notes, pens and receipts, all thrown in together. Before you can find anything, ==you sort it==. Document parsing does that for documents.

items.label: Don't think
items.text: PDF → Text → AI

items.label: Think
items.text: PDF → Structure → AI

body.text: Docling or MinerU, the idea is the same: turn messy documents into structured information that software and AI can work with. That's the whole game.

body.label: Go deeper: read the Docling post

body.text: **Also read:** [ColBERT: When Normal Semantic Search Isn't Enough](/blog/colbert-when-semantic-search-isnt-enough), the next step: finding the right passages once your documents are parsed.

title: Your PDF Isn't Just Text. That's Why AI Can Struggle With It.
excerpt: Pull the text out of a PDF and the structure falls apart: headings, tables, reading order. Here's how Docling keeps it, and where it fits in a RAG system.

image.alt: From messy documents to useful AI answers, in six steps: 1, a PDF (a sample quarterly report with text, a table, an image and a chart); 2, Docling analyses layout, reading order, tables, images, sections and runs OCR on scans; 3, structured content (heading, paragraph, table, image, chart, section); 4, chunks; 5, embeddings turn chunks into vectors; 6, a RAG app answers "What was the revenue in Q3 2024?" with the right figure and its source. Better document structure leads to better AI answers; Docling is the document-understanding step, not the whole RAG system.

body.text: Say you have a 100-page PDF and you want an AI to answer questions about it. The obvious plan is to extract the text and hand it over.
Then you look at what came out.
**What plain text extraction gave you:**

body.code:
Revenue
2025
Company A 120
Company B 98
Company C 143
...

body.text: The headings are mixed in with the paragraphs. The table has lost its shape. The images are gone, and the reading order can come out wrong. A document that looked neatly organised to you has turned into a pile of words.
That's the problem Docling was built for.
▶ [Watch my 4-minute Docling walkthrough](#video-pdYdzpQQcCc)
What's actually inside a PDF

body.alt: A PDF is not just text. Left: a sample quarterly business review as you see it. Middle: the elements it contains, each with a different meaning: heading, text, image, table, chart and layout. Right: a structured document representation where each element is identified and organised: heading, paragraph, image, table, chart, section and footer.
body.caption: The example report in these pictures is made up.

body.text: A PDF looks like a simple page, but it holds many different things: headings, paragraphs, tables, images, lists, captions, headers and footers, sections, and a page layout with a reading order that ties them together.
When you look at a page, your brain sorts this out without effort. This is the title. This paragraph belongs under that heading. These numbers are a table. That picture is a figure.
A basic text extractor doesn't necessarily keep any of those relationships. That matters, because everything after it, including the AI, only sees what the extractor hands over.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: A PDF is a structured document, not just text.
What Docling does

body.alt: Docling turns messy documents into structured content. 1, a messy PDF as input; 2, Docling processing: layout analysis, reading order, detecting tables and images, understanding sections and handling scanned PDFs with OCR; 3, a structured DoclingDocument as output (heading, paragraph, image, table with header and rows, chart, section, footer), ready to export as Markdown, JSON or HTML.

body.text: Docling is an open-source tool that converts documents into a structured representation instead of one long string of text. It was started by the AI for knowledge team at IBM Research Zurich, it's MIT licensed, and it now lives under the LF AI & Data Foundation.

Its core format is called [DoclingDocument](https://github.com/docling-project/docling/blob/main/docs/concepts/docling_document.md). It can hold text, tables, pictures, the heading hierarchy, layout information and reading order. So instead of a flat pile of words you get something closer to a tree:

body.code:
Document
 ├── Section
 │    ├── Heading
 │    ├── Paragraph
 │    └── Table
 │         ├── Header
 │         ├── Row
 │         └── Row
 └── Figure

body.label: Good to know
body.text: Docling isn't only for PDFs. It also reads DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML and images, among other formats.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Docling keeps the document's structure instead of flattening it.
It reads the layout, not just the words

body.alt: Docling understands the layout of your document. Left: the original PDF page. Middle: the structure Docling detected, with a numbered box around each part: 1 heading, 2 paragraph, 3 image, 4 table, 5 section, 6 chart, 7 footer. Right: the list of detected elements and the reading order, from heading to footer.

body.text: Before Docling can label anything, it has to work out what's on the page. It analyses the layout, finds each element (heading, paragraph, image, table, section, chart, footer) and works out the reading order, so a two-column page isn't read straight across.
In the picture, every detected element gets a numbered box, and the list on the right shows the order it would be read in: heading first, then paragraph, image, table, and so on.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: It doesn't just read words. It finds and labels the parts of the page.
What about scanned PDFs?
Some PDFs contain no selectable text at all. They're pictures of pages. Try to select a word and nothing happens.

That's where OCR comes in. Optical character recognition looks at the pixels and recognises the text inside them. Docling supports OCR with several engines to choose from, such as Tesseract, EasyOCR and RapidOCR. On the command line it's switched on by default, and there's a --force-ocr option if you want it on every page.
But OCR only finds letters. Docling's layout steps are what decide what those letters are: a heading, a table cell, a caption.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: OCR reads the pixels. Layout analysis works out what they mean.
Getting the words is not the same as keeping the document

body.alt: Getting the words is not the same as understanding the document. 1, basic text extraction: the PDF becomes plain lines of text and numbers; all content is flattened and tables, layout and hierarchy are lost. 2, Docling's structure-aware parsing: a heading, a paragraph, a table with its rows and columns, an image and a chart, exported as Markdown, JSON or HTML. Structure is preserved.

body.text: Here's the comparison that matters. Basic extraction hands you the words: Revenue, 2024, Product, Revenue, A, 120, B, 98, C, 143. They're all there, but whatever reads them next has to guess which number belongs to which product.
Docling hands you the same content with its shape: a heading, a paragraph, a table with columns, rows and cells, a figure, a section.

Then you choose how to get it out. The [command line](https://docling-project.github.io/docling/reference/cli/) exports Markdown by default, and it also does JSON, YAML, HTML, plain text, DocTags and chunks. A table stays a table:

body.code:
# Annual Revenue

## 2025 Results

The company reported...

| Product | Revenue |
|---------|---------|
| A       | 120     |
| B       | 98      |
| C       | 143     |

body.text: That's much more useful to an LLM than a flattened wall of words.
**Try it yourself.** Install it and convert a PDF from the command line:

body.code:
pip install docling
docling report.pdf

body.text: Or do the same in Python:

body.code:
from docling.document_converter import DocumentConverter

result = DocumentConverter().convert("report.pdf")
print(result.document.export_to_markdown())

body.text: **Watch it run.** I recorded a walkthrough of Docling. You can also [watch it on YouTube](https://youtu.be/pdYdzpQQcCc).

body.title: Docling (Uma's walkthrough video)
body.caption: Docling · 4:04

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Getting the words is not the same as keeping the document.
Where RAG comes in
Docling is not RAG. RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, is a whole pipeline where an AI looks up the relevant pieces of your documents before it answers. Docling is one early stage of it.

It prepares the document. The later stages decide how that information is chunked, embedded, stored and retrieved. Docling can help with chunking too: it has hybrid and hierarchical chunkers, and the command line can export chunks directly with --to chunks.

Here's why it matters. Imagine you upload a company's annual report and ask, "What was the revenue of Product B in 2025?" If the table was destroyed during extraction, the AI has to guess which number belongs to which product. If the structure survived, the rest of the pipeline has much better information to work with.
That's why document processing isn't a boring step hiding in the basement. It changes what your AI system has to work with.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Docling gets the document ready. RAG uses it to answer questions.

body.label: One thing to be careful about
body.text: You might hear Docling described as a tool that "extracts everything without missing anything". Don't repeat that. No document parser can honestly promise it for every PDF, scan, table, font or layout, and results depend on the document and the settings. A safer way to say it: Docling is designed to extract a document's content while keeping as much of its structure as it can. Run it on your own documents and check the output before you rely on it.
The mental model to remember

items.label: Don't think
items.text: PDF → Text → AI

items.label: Think
items.text: PDF → Document understanding → Structured data → AI

items: Docling: heading, paragraph, table, image, section, reading order

body.text: A PDF isn't just text. It's a structured document, and Docling's job is to turn it into structured information your AI pipeline can use.

body.alt: From messy documents to useful AI answers, in six steps: 1, a PDF (a sample quarterly report with text, a table, an image and a chart); 2, Docling analyses layout, reading order, tables, images, sections and runs OCR on scans; 3, structured content (heading, paragraph, table, image, chart, section); 4, chunks; 5, embeddings turn chunks into vectors; 6, a RAG app answers "What was the revenue in Q3 2024?" with the right figure and its source. Better document structure leads to better AI answers; Docling is the document-understanding step, not the whole RAG system.
body.caption: The whole journey on one page. Click to enlarge.

body.text: **Also read:** [Docling and MinerU: A Simple Guide to Document Parsing](/blog/mineru-document-parsing-for-beginners), a lighter introduction that compares Docling with MinerU, and [ColBERT: When Normal Semantic Search Isn't Enough](/blog/colbert-when-semantic-search-isnt-enough), on finding the right passages.

title: AI Can Write the Code. So What Happens to Software Development?
excerpt: AI made coding fast. Now everything around the code is the slow part. Here's the whole journey from idea to app, one picture at a time.

image.alt: The AI-native SDLC on one page: six stages from idea to real app, Plan, Design, Build, Test, Deploy and Maintain, with real user feedback looping back to planning. AI speeds up the work; humans make the important decisions.

body.text: Ask an AI for a login screen and you'll have one in under a minute. Ask for a database, a set of tests, a whole feature, and it keeps going.
So typing the code is no longer the hard part. What is?

That's the question behind a [playbook Anthropic published](https://claude.com/blog/the-ai-native-sdlc-playbook) on the "AI-native SDLC". SDLC just means the software development life cycle: every step a product goes through, from an idea in your head to an app people use, and back again.
What actually changed

body.alt: Before AI vs With AI. Before: you do everything manually and coding takes about 20 hours of the whole journey. With AI: AI helps you write code fast, coding takes about 1 hour, and review and maintenance become visible steps. When coding gets faster, the bottleneck moves.

body.text: For years, writing the code ate most of a project's time. The hours in the picture are illustrative, but you'll recognise the shape. In the top row, coding is one long red bar. In the bottom row, AI shrinks it to almost nothing, and suddenly testing, reviewing and deploying are the longest steps.
When code stops being the bottleneck, the bottleneck moves to planning, reviewing and shipping, which still run at human speed.
That's the playbook's main point in one line. The rest of this post walks through each stage and what it looks like now, using one running example: a habit tracker for students.
Plan: decide what you're actually building

body.alt: Plan: a messy idea (a habit tracker for students) goes through key questions (who is it for, what should it do, any limits) and becomes a clear one-page plan with target users, main features and constraints.

body.text: "Build me a habit tracker" is a wish, not a plan. An AI will happily build something from it, just not necessarily what you had in mind.

Before any code, answer three questions: who is it for, what must it do, and what are the limits? For our tracker: college students aged 18 to 25; track daily habits, send reminders and show streaks; Android and iOS, free and simple.

body.label: From the playbook
body.text: Anthropic's version of this step ends with a short file called intent.md: the problem, who has it, what success looks like and what's still open. The AI helps draft it and a person approves it. The aim is to go from first conversation to an agreed plan in hours, not weeks.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: If you can't explain your app in five lines, the AI can't build it.
Design: screens, flow and tech in one sitting

body.alt: Design: turn your idea into a clear design in three parts: what it looks like (the app screens), how it works (open app, mark habit, track progress, stay motivated) and how we build it (Flutter, Supabase, OpenAI, Vercel).

body.text: Now decide what it looks like and how it works: the screens (home, add a habit, progress), the path a user takes through them (open the app, tick a habit, watch the streak grow), and the tools you'll build it with.
The picture shows one set of choices, Flutter with Supabase. Any stack works. What matters is that the choice is written down.

body.label: From the playbook
body.text: Requirements and design used to be separate phases, run by separate teams. In the AI-native version they happen in one session: the AI turns the plan into a spec, checks it against the team's rules on security, branding and privacy, and flags anything that needs a human decision.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: AI follows a clear design far better than a vague idea.
Build: you direct, AI types, you review

body.alt: Build: 1, give the plan; 2, AI builds the app (screens, database, tests); 3, review the result. You give direction, AI does much of the implementation, you review and guide.

body.text: This is the part everyone pictures. You hand over the plan, and the AI writes the screens, database tables, login and tests.
What changes is your job. You spend less time typing every line and more time giving direction and checking what comes back.

body.label: From the playbook
body.text: Even here, planning comes first. The AI proposes which files will change, in what order and with which tests, and the engineer approves that before any code is written. Team knowledge lives in a file the AI reads every time, with rules like "money is always BigDecimal, never double".

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: The better your plan and your review, the better the code.
Test: catch problems while they're small

body.alt: Don't wait until the end to find problems: AI runs 10 tests, finds 1 problem, fixes it, runs all tests again, and you quickly review the result and keep building.

body.text: "AI wrote it" doesn't mean "it works". In the picture, ten checks pass and one fails: the reminder doesn't fire. The AI finds the cause, fixes it, runs everything again, and only then does a person look.
It's like building a house. You check the door fits while the frame is going up, not after the walls are painted.

body.label: From the playbook
body.text: The AI gets one command that runs every check, and it keeps going until they all pass. The tests themselves are locked, so the AI can't "fix" a failure by quietly editing the test.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Test early, fix fast, keep moving.
Deploy: from your laptop to real users
Working on your laptop isn't the same as working for thousands of people. Deploy is the step where your app leaves your machine.
AI can prepare most of it: open the change, run automated reviews for bugs and security, and fix what they find. The final yes stays with a person.

body.label: From the playbook
body.text: The AI can write a change request but can't approve its own. The rules tighten with risk: free rein while developing, some limits in testing, and a human sign-off for anything going to production.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Automate the checks. Keep a human on the release button.
Maintain: launch is where the loop starts

body.alt: Maintain: software is a loop, not a one-time project. Real people use your app, users report problems, AI investigates, a human checks, you fix and improve, release an update, then learn from users and plan again.

body.text: The app is live. Time to relax? Not quite.

Real users arrive with real problems. One says it crashes. One says it's slow. One asks for dark mode. Each of these goes round the same loop: AI investigates, a person decides the fix, it's built, tested and shipped, and what you learned feeds the next plan.

body.label: From the playbook
body.text: Monitoring watches the numbers and calls the AI when something drifts. The AI writes up what it found in the same format as a new idea, so a bug in production re-enters the pipeline at stage 1. A person still decides what gets fixed.

body.label: Takeaway
body.text: Software is a loop, not a one-time project.
So what actually changed?

body.alt: The AI-native SDLC on one page: six stages from idea to real app, Plan, Design, Build, Test, Deploy and Maintain, with real user feedback looping back to planning. AI speeds up the work; humans make the important decisions.

items.label: The old picture
items.text: A developer writes code, and the app gets built.

items.label: The new picture
items.text: A person sets the goal. AI helps plan, build and test. People review. The app reaches users, AI helps watch it, and what users say becomes the next idea.

body.text: Where your time goes now
The biggest change isn't speed. It's where your attention goes.

items.label: Less
items.text: "How do I write this by hand?"

items.label: More
items.text:
What should we build?
Is it useful?
Did the AI build the right thing?
What could go wrong?
What are users telling us?

body.text: People don't disappear from this picture. They move up: less typing, more deciding.

title: How AI Actually Learns: I Taught a Computer With My Own Images
excerpt: I taught Google's Teachable Machine to tell my spectacles from my phone in a few minutes, then tried to break it. Here's what that shows about how machine learning really works.

image.alt: Infographic of the whole experiment: How AI actually learns, in 5 minutes with your webcam.

learn: How a computer learns from examples instead of rules
The difference between training and inference
Why a model breaks when the situation changes, and what that says about your data
Why tools like this train in seconds (transfer learning)

items: Everywhere we look, someone is talking about AI.
ChatGPT. Face unlock. Recommendation systems. Self-driving cars.
But there is one question that gets surprisingly confusing when you first enter AI:

body.text: How does a computer actually learn?

items.text: You can read about neural networks for hours.
Or you can teach one yourself in a few minutes.

body.text: That's what I did with Google's [Teachable Machine](/toolkit/teachable). It runs in the browser and lets you create simple machine-learning models using images, sounds, or poses.
And this tiny experiment made the basic idea of machine learning much easier for me to understand.
First, See the Whole Thing
Before getting into the individual steps, look at this image.

body.alt: Infographic: How AI actually learns in 5 minutes with your webcam. Ten panels: open Teachable Machine, create two classes (phone and empty hand), record examples, train the model, test it (98% phone), break it with a TV remote (92% phone), see what it actually learned (same room, same hand, similar background), change the situation (left hand, low light, far away), the big idea (it finds patterns in your examples) and why it trains so fast (transfer learning).
body.caption: The whole experiment on one page. Click to enlarge.

body.text: Think of this image as the map for the entire experiment:

items: You don't even need to read the article yet.
Want to see the whole experiment?

body.title: Teachable Machine walkthrough (1:23)
body.caption: ▶ The full Teachable Machine walkthrough. It's about 1 minute 23 seconds, and it shows the actual process from beginning to prediction.

body.text: Now let's break down what happened.
Step 1: Open Teachable Machine
Start at the Teachable Machine homepage.
The idea is simple:
You give the computer examples, and it learns to distinguish between them.
Click **Get Started**.

body.alt: Step 1: the Teachable Machine homepage, with an arrow pointing to the blue Get Started button.

body.text: No Python.
No installing libraries.
No terminal.
We're just going to experiment.
Step 2: Choose What You Want the Computer to Learn
Teachable Machine gives you different types of projects.
You can teach it using:
For this experiment, we want images.
So choose **Image Project**.

body.alt: Step 2: the New Project screen with Image Project, Audio Project and Pose Project; an arrow points to Image Project.

body.text: This is already an important ML idea.
We're defining what kind of information the model is going to learn from.
In our case:
Step 3: Choose the Image Model
You'll see options for the image model.
For a normal beginner experiment, choose the **Standard Image Model**.

body.alt: Step 3: the New Image Project dialog with Standard image model and Embedded image model; an arrow points to Standard image model.

body.text: Don't get stuck on the technical details here.
We're not trying to build the next computer-vision research system.
We're trying to understand one thing:
How can examples teach a machine to recognize something?
That is today's experiment.
Step 4: Create Your Classes
Now the interesting part begins.
A class simply means:
“This is category A.”
and
“This is category B.”
In our experiment, let's use:

body.alt: Step 4: two classes named Spectacles and Phone, each with an Upload button, and notes to upload images of different spectacles and different smartphones.

body.text: Now we're essentially telling the system:
“These are the two things I want you to learn to distinguish.”
This is where machine learning starts feeling less mysterious.
We're not writing a giant list of rules like:

body.code:
If shape = this
and color = this
and position = this
then it's a phone.

body.text: We're providing examples.
Step 5: Give It Examples
Now we need to actually teach it.
Click **Upload** and give the first class examples of spectacles.
Then do the same for the phone class.

body.alt: Step 5: the upload panel for Class 1, with the “Choose images from your files” button highlighted for uploading pictures of spectacles.

body.text: For example:

items: **Spectacles class:** upload several images of spectacles.
**Phone class:** upload several images of phones.

body.alt: Moving on to Class 2: an arrow points to its Upload button to add phone images, with a reminder that no class should be left empty.

body.text: And here's where something very important is happening.
You aren't giving the model a definition of a phone.
You're giving it examples of phones.
You aren't explaining:
“A phone is a rectangular electronic device with a screen.”
You're simply saying:
“Here are examples that belong to Class 2.”
That's the fundamental idea we want to understand.
Step 6: More Examples Don't Automatically Mean Better
Imagine you give the model only one photo of spectacles.
Then you give it one photo of a phone.
It has very little information to work with.
Now imagine you give it many examples.
Now it has more variety to learn from.
This leads to one of the biggest lessons in machine learning:

body.label: Key idea
body.text: The quality and variety of your training examples matter.
The model can only learn patterns that exist in the data you give it.
That's why real machine learning datasets are such a big deal.
Step 7: Train the Model
Now comes the button everyone wants to press.
**Train Model**.

body.alt: Step 7: both classes have images, and an arrow points to the Train Model button in the Training panel.

body.text: Click it.
Wait.
And now the model has been trained using the examples you provided.
This is the moment where people often imagine:
“The AI has now understood what a phone is.”
Not quite.
And this is where things get interesting.
Step 8: Let's Test It
Once training is finished, the model gives you a live prediction.
Point the webcam at something from your training examples.
You'll see probabilities for the different classes.

body.alt: Step 8: the trained model's webcam preview. The output shows 39% for Class 1 and 61% for Class 2, with arrows explaining that the model matched the object to Class 2.

body.text: For example:
The model is basically saying:
“Based on what I learned from the examples, this input looks more like Class 2.”
That prediction is called **inference**.
You don't need to memorize that word yet.
Just remember:

items.title: Training
items.text: Learn from examples.

items.title: Inference
items.text: Use what was learned to make a prediction.

body.text: That's a very important distinction in AI.
Now Let's Break the Model
This is my favorite part.
Don't just show the model the exact examples you trained it on.
Try to fool it.

items: Show it something that looks visually similar.

body.text: And watch what happens.
Because now we're asking the real question:

body.label: The real question
body.text: Did the model actually learn the thing we wanted it to learn? Or did it simply find some patterns in our training examples?
What Did It Actually Learn?
This is where the experiment becomes machine learning.
Suppose every phone image you uploaded had:

items: the phone in roughly the same position
your hand appearing in the same way

body.text: You might think:
“I taught it what a phone looks like.”
But the model doesn't know what “phone” means in the human sense.
It is learning patterns from the input examples.
So some patterns you never intended to teach can become useful to the model.
That's why changing the situation can make the prediction worse.
And suddenly we get a much better understanding of why training data matters.
This Is the Core Machine Learning Loop
Look at the big image again.

body.alt: Infographic: How AI actually learns in 5 minutes with your webcam. Ten panels: open Teachable Machine, create two classes (phone and empty hand), record examples, train the model, test it (98% phone), break it with a TV remote (92% phone), see what it actually learned (same room, same hand, similar background), change the situation (left hand, low light, far away), the big idea (it finds patterns in your examples) and why it trains so fast (transfer learning).
body.caption: The whole experiment on one page. Click to enlarge.

body.text: You can reduce the whole experiment to this:
That's the basic loop.
Not all of modern AI works exactly like this, but this experiment gives you the intuition behind supervised learning and classification.
And Then There Is the Sneaky Problem
Imagine you trained the model using:
Now you test:
The model may struggle.
Why?
Because your original data had a pattern you didn't realize was there.
You wanted it to learn:
**Phone vs Spectacles.**
But your examples may have accidentally taught it:
**Right-hand setup vs table setup.**
This is why good training data matters.
And this is also why testing only on the same kind of examples used during training can give you a false sense that everything is perfect.
So Why Did This Train So Quickly?
This is another cool part of the experiment.
You didn't spend six hours training a giant model from zero.
You clicked a button and got a result in a browser.
One reason is **transfer learning**.
Think about it like this.
Imagine hiring an artist who already knows how to recognize:
You don't need to teach them what a shape is from scratch.
You just give them a new task:
“Now help me separate these two categories.”
That's the basic intuition behind transfer learning.
Instead of starting from zero, an already-trained model can provide useful learned representations, and you adapt it for your smaller task.
That is one of the reasons tools like this can make experimentation so fast.
You Just Saw Machine Learning Without the Math
And that's actually the point.
You didn't need to start with:
Those concepts become important later.
But before learning all of that, I think it's useful to understand the basic story first.
A machine-learning model gets examples.
It learns patterns from those examples.
You give it something new.
It makes a prediction.
Then you test whether those predictions actually work outside the examples it saw.
That's the idea you just watched happen.
